FrMS88-d1e411-d1e111.summary: Incipit rubric of the Venice 1519 edition, announcing the 'conflatus' commentary of the 'illuminated doctor' Francis of Meyronnes, OFM, on the first book of the Sentences, and marking the beginning of question 1.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e127.summary: States the first question of the prologue on the opening of Lombard's first book ('Cupientes'): whether a first complex principle can be formed in theology. The opening negative argument appeals to Dionysius: those who think rightly of God both attribute all things to him and remove all things from him, which seems to undermine any first principle (such as non-contradiction) applied to God.
claims: Dionysius' teaching that all things are both affirmed and denied of God seems to exclude a first complex principle in theology.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e153.summary: Argument to the contrary, also from Dionysius: Scripture proceeds in two ordered ways, from affirmations to negations and from negations to affirmations, which presupposes ordered and distinct affirmation and negation, and thus the first principle.
claims: Scripture's twofold process between affirmations and negations presupposes their distinctness.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e169.summary: Divides the question into two principal tasks: first, to declare (explain) the first principle; second, to defend it.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e175.summary: Subdivides the first task: the first principle will be explained first in itself and second in comparison with theology.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e182.summary: Further subdivides the explanation of the principle in itself into a general treatment and a specific treatment.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e187.summary: Introduces four preambles for the general explanation of the first principle and gives the first: the first complex principle is formed about the first subject. The proof rests on the parallel between the order of wholes and the order of their essential parts; since propositions are wholes composed of terms, the first proposition must be composed of the first terms, and the first term is the first subject.
claims: The order of propositions arises from the order of their terms.
The first complex principle is formed about the first subject.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e216.summary: Second preamble: the first complex principle enters into the first demonstration, by the same whole–part reasoning: demonstrations are wholes composed of propositions, so the first demonstration contains the first proposition as an essential part.
claims: The first complex principle is an essential part of the first demonstration.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e232.summary: Third preamble: the first principle yields the first conclusion simply speaking, since a scientific conclusion is the effect of its principles and the first effect proceeds from the first cause.
claims: The first conclusion is derived from the first principle as an effect from its first cause.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e243.summary: Fourth preamble: the first principle is formed in the first science. Since sciences are distinguished and ordered by their subjects, and the first science concerns the first subject about which the first principle is formed, the first science begins its process from that principle.
claims: Sciences are distinguished and ordered by their subjects.
The first principle belongs to the first science, whose process begins from it.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e260.summary: Draws from the preambles four properties of the first complex principle and gives the first: it is most common (universal), since it is composed of the first and most universal terms.
claims: The first complex principle is the most universal of principles.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e273.summary: Second property: the first principle is intimate and intrinsic to all things, because universals are intrinsic to the inferiors over which they extend, and this principle is composed of the most universal terms extending to everything.
claims: The first principle is intrinsic to everything to which its universal terms extend.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e282.summary: Third property: the first principle is in itself most true, because, according to Augustine's De vera religione, the eternal rules are immutable and most true, and this principle is the foremost of those rules.
claims: The first principle is the foremost of the immutable eternal rules and hence most true.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e298.summary: Fourth property: the first principle is in itself most known, since all knowledge derives from the evidence either of the proposition or of its terms, and the terms of this principle are the most universal and simple, hence most known.
claims: A proposition composed of the most known terms is itself most known.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e311.summary: Introduces four conclusions explaining the first principle and gives the first: in the whole order of principles there must be one first complex principle, since, just as among causes there must be a first to avoid an infinite regress, so among principles and what is derived from them.
claims: There is a first complex principle in the order of principles, on pain of infinite regress.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e331.summary: Confirms the first conclusion: among essentially ordered things there must be a first.
claims: In essentially ordered series a first member is necessary.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e337.summary: Second conclusion: the first principle is unique. Just as among simple beings there cannot be two simply first beings (the argument used to establish the unity of the first principle of being), so among complexes there cannot be two simply first propositions.
claims: The first complex principle is unique, by analogy with the uniqueness of the first being.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e348.summary: Confirms the second conclusion: every essential order is related to some one first; since there is an essential order among propositions, one proposition must be uniquely first.
claims: Every essential order has a unique first term.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e359.summary: Third conclusion: the first principle extends to everything to which the formal notion of its terms extends. The habitude grounding its truth arises immediately from the notions of its terms, its predicate being included in its subject, so wherever its subject is, the whole principle is found.
claims: The first principle holds wherever its subject is found, because its truth arises immediately from the notions of its terms.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e377.summary: Fourth conclusion, first proof: the truth of the first principle can only be found where its terms are found, since its truth consists in a habitude between terms, and a habitude cannot exist without its extremes.
claims: The truth of the first principle cannot exist without its terms.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e393.summary: Second proof of the fourth conclusion: a whole cannot be found without its parts, and the first principle is constituted as a whole from its terms.
claims: The first principle, as a whole composed of terms, exists only where its terms exist.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e400.summary: Turns to the specific treatment of the first principle and identifies it: 'Of anything, the affirmation or the negation is true, and of nothing are both true together' — the formula commonly accepted as the first principle.
claims: The first complex principle is: of anything the affirmation or negation is true, and of nothing both together.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e414.summary: First of four conclusions clarifying the principle: the whole principle is a single hypothetical, copulative proposition containing two categoricals — a universal affirmative with a disjunctive predicate (of everything, affirmation or negation) and a universal negative with a copulative predicate (of nothing, affirmation and negation together).
claims: The first principle is one copulative hypothetical proposition composed of a universal affirmative with disjunctive predicate and a universal negative with copulative predicate.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e434.summary: Second conclusion: the two parts of the principle are ordered as commonly stated, the universal affirmative being prior to the universal negative, since when affirmation and negation concern the same terms the affirmative is prior, every negation being reducible to an affirmation.
claims: Of an affirmation and negation about the same terms, the affirmation is prior.
The affirmative part of the first principle is prior to the negative part.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e450.summary: Applies the rule to the case: the disjunctive categorical part is affirmative and the copulative part negative, so the affirmative part is prior.
claims: The disjunctive part of the first principle is affirmative and therefore prior.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e457.summary: Confirms the order: of propositions related as antecedent and consequent one is prior; the copulative about the same terms always implies the disjunctive and not conversely, so the affirmative (disjunctive) part is the prior one.
claims: Logical implication between the two parts establishes their order.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e468.summary: Third conclusion: the subject of the first complex principle is being (ens), since the most common proposition has the most common subject, and being is the most common subject.
claims: Being (ens) is the subject of the first complex principle.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e484.summary: Confirms that being is the subject: the principle contains the adjectives 'of anything' and 'of nothing', which require an understood substantive, and in such expressions 'thing' or 'being' is understood.
claims: The quantifiers 'quolibet' and 'nullo' presuppose an understood substantive, namely being.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e494.summary: Fourth conclusion: the predicate of the principle is affirmation or negation, taken as a disjunct attribute in the first part (as even or odd are disjunct properties of number) and as affirmation and negation copulatively in the second part. This is proved because in the most powerful demonstration a property is concluded of its subject, so affirmation and negation function as properties predicated of being.
claims: Affirmation and negation function as disjunct properties (passiones) of being in the first principle.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e512.summary: Raises four objections against the four conclusions; the first, against the first conclusion, argues that the principle is really several principles because opposite conclusions (affirmative and negative) can be inferred from it.
claims: Objection: since opposite conclusions follow from it, the first principle is plural rather than one.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e521.summary: Second objection, against the second conclusion: where two truths are essentially ordered, the posterior can be deduced from the prior; but then the negative part would be deduced from the affirmative and would not be per se known nor a first principle.
claims: Objection: if the negative part is posterior, it would be derivable and not a first principle.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e532.summary: Third objection, against the third conclusion: the principle is verified of the simply simple and the primarily diverse, in which being is not included; hence being is not its subject.
claims: Objection: the first principle extends to things in which being is not quidditatively included, so being is not its subject.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e539.summary: Fourth objection, against the fourth conclusion: affirmation and negation belong to logic, whereas the first principle belongs to the metaphysician; hence its predicate cannot be affirmation and negation.
claims: Objection: affirmation and negation are logical items, while the first principle is metaphysical.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e550.summary: Reply to the first objection: the first principle is one not by the unity of simplicity but by the unity of a certain integrity, in the manner of a hypothetical proposition.
claims: The first principle has the unity of an integral whole, not of a simple.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e558.summary: Reply to the second objection: the posterior is deducible from the prior only when one truth can be subsumed under another as a conclusion under premises; this is impossible when both propositions share the same terms and differ only by their signs (copulation and disjunction), as here.
claims: Propositions with identical terms differing only in their logical signs cannot be deduced one from the other as conclusion from premises.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e571.summary: Reply to the third objection: being is included in the simply simple and primarily diverse denominatively (as an adjective) but not quidditatively; the principle is truly verified of them, though not quidditatively, just as 'a man is white or not white' is true without being quidditatively necessary.
claims: Being is said of the simply simple and primarily diverse denominatively, not quidditatively.
The first principle need not be verified quidditatively to be true of a thing.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e589.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: second intentions sometimes supposit for first intentions (as when a definition is said to be predicated of the defined); affirmation and negation are the predicate of the first principle only as suppositing for first intentions, namely being and non-being.
claims: In the first principle, 'affirmation' and 'negation' supposit for being and non-being.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e598.summary: Raises a further objection: the principle extends to privations and fictions (anything is blindness or not blindness, chimera or not chimera), which are not called beings; so being is not its subject.
claims: Objection: the first principle applies to privations and fictions, which are not beings.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e607.summary: Replies that privations and fictions do not wholly escape the notion of being, being beings of reason; or better, that they are beings only in a qualified sense, and the principle is found in them likewise only in a qualified and quasi-fictive sense.
claims: Privations and fictions are beings secundum quid, and the first principle holds of them only secundum quid.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e620.summary: Introduces a second instance against the reply to the third objection, namely that being is said of the primarily diverse only denominatively (like the other attributes of being) and that this suffices to save the first principle in them.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e630.summary: First of four arguments against that reply: take the formal notion of goodness; either it is quidditatively good or not. If so, something is said quidditatively of an attribute of being; if not, there is an infinite regress of goods of goods. Hence the principle extends to the simply simple quidditatively, not merely by denomination.
claims: The first principle seems to apply quidditatively to the attributes of being, not merely denominatively.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e646.summary: Second argument: the disjunction 'the formal notion of goodness is either quidditatively primarily diverse or not' belongs to the first principle.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e653.summary: Third argument: the disjunction 'the notion of goodness is either quidditatively simply simple or not' likewise falls under the first principle.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e658.summary: Fourth argument: the notion of goodness is either quidditatively a being or quidditatively a non-being.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e665.summary: Reply to the first argument: 'goodness is quidditatively good' should be granted, and so the whole disjunction; yet there is no quidditative complexity there except one fashioned by the mind, since there is only one formal term, so the first complex principle does not properly apply.
claims: Where there is only one formal term, a complex holds only as fashioned by the mind, so the first complex principle does not properly apply.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e681.summary: Reply to the second (and implicitly third) argument: goodness is not quidditatively primarily diverse, because diversity expresses a respect not belonging to the quiddity of anything absolute; similarly simplicity, perhaps a negation (lack of composability), is not said quidditatively of anything positive.
claims: Diversity is a respect and not part of the quiddity of an absolute.
Simplicity is a negation and is not said quidditatively of anything positive.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e695.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: the disjunction is to be granted, but it does not belong to the first complex principle.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e700.summary: Draws two rules from the principle; the first, from its first (disjunctive) part: of any contradiction one part is necessarily true.
claims: Of every contradictory pair, one part is necessarily true.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e709.summary: Gives the second rule (contradictories cannot be true together) and turns to the principle in relation to theology, first applying the first rule. Introduces four conclusions and gives the first: the principle or its truth is formally found in creatures, since wherever a conclusion deduced from the first principle is found the principle is found, and disjunctions such as 'necessary or not necessary' are true of creatures.
claims: Contradictories cannot be simultaneously true.
The truth of the first principle is formally found in creatures.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e740.summary: Second conclusion: the truth of the first principle is formally found and holds in God, since conclusions of the principle such as 'God is eternal or not eternal' are true of God.
claims: The first principle formally holds in God.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e749.summary: Third conclusion: the principle is found in God and creatures under the same notion. A proposition whose subject includes incompossibles cannot be true; 'God is eternal or not eternal' presupposes 'of any being, affirmation or negation is true', and the universal sign must attach to a universal term common to God and creatures, not a singular one, else it would include incompossibles.
claims: The first principle applies to God and creatures under the same formal notion.
A universal sign joined to a singular term yields an incompossible subject.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e773.summary: Further argument: when terms under the same formal notion extend to certain things, so does the complex principle formed from them; affirmation and negation (e.g. eternal or not eternal) are said disjunctively of God and creatures, hence so is the subject, and thus the first principle.
claims: Since the disjunctive predicate is common to God and creatures, so is the subject and the first principle.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e787.summary: Confirmation: the predicate of the first principle is adequate to its subject; since every disjunctive affirmation and negation said of God is said of creatures, the subject is common, and where subject and predicate are the same the proposition is the same; so the same first principle holds in God and creatures.
claims: The predicate of the first principle is adequate to its subject.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e798.summary: Fourth conclusion, following from the third: since the principle is found in God and creatures under the same formal notion, one and the same principle is found in both.
claims: One and the same first principle holds in God and in creatures.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e805.summary: Confirmation: whatever has one part of a contradiction verified of it has both parts verified disjunctively; since for any contradiction one part is true of God and of creatures, the disjunction is said of both, showing the same first principle holds in each.
claims: Any contradiction holds disjunctively of both God and creatures.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e823.summary: Confirms the preceding by Augustine (De Trinitate I) that some rules hold only of God, some only of creatures, and some of both, such as 'nothing generates itself' — a fortiori the first principle. Then turns to the second rule (contradictories cannot be verified of the same) and reports the view that it does not hold in divine matters because of the infinity of the divine essence, which can be both communicable and incommunicable, supported by Dionysius' Mystical Theology that the affirmations and negations about God are not contrary.
claims: Some rules hold of both God and creatures.
Reported view: because of divine infinity, the principle of non-contradiction fails in God.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e860.summary: Adds a second support for that view — the theologians' saying that the same thing is attributed and denied of God by distinct reasons — and then begins four arguments against it. First: the most evident complex truth cannot conflict with the first incomplex truth, since the order of propositions follows the order of things; the first complex principle is the most evident complex truth and the divine truth the first incomplex truth.
claims: The most evident complex truth cannot be repugnant to the first incomplex truth (God).

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e876.summary: Confirmation: removing what everything else presupposes removes everything else; all our natural knowledge presupposes the first complex principle, so if it is removed from God we could have no natural knowledge of God.
claims: Denying the first principle in God would destroy all natural knowledge of God.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e886.summary: Second argument: things incompossible by their formal notions remain incompossible to whatever subject they are applied, as long as their notions remain; the extremes of a contradiction are incompossible by their formal notions.
claims: Contradictories remain incompossible in any subject, including God.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e899.summary: Third argument: the more intense things are which are repugnant of themselves, the more intense their repugnance; hence in the most perfect nature, where they are most intense, contradictories are supremely repugnant.
claims: In the most perfect nature contradictories are maximally repugnant.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e910.summary: Fourth argument: if the infinity of the subject removed one repugnance it would remove all, so 'God is eternal and not eternal' or 'infinite and not infinite' would not conflict, and no heretic could be refuted, since he could concede both parts of a contradiction.
claims: If infinity suspended non-contradiction, heresy could not be refuted.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e921.summary: Concludes that neither infinity nor mere distinction of reason can save the contradiction found in God, since the contradictories there arise from the nature of the thing. Reports the view of an 'excellent colleague' who, wishing to save the principle without a formal distinction, holds that essence and relation are one thing with distinct definitions, as action and passion are one motion, or similarity and dissimilarity are distinct species of relation founded on one whiteness; distinct definitions would save the contradiction.
claims: Neither divine infinity nor a mere distinction of reason saves contradictions that arise ex natura rei.
Reported view: essence and relation in God are one thing with distinct definitions, which suffices to avoid contradiction.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e947.summary: From the colleague's 'very welcome' sayings derives four conclusions for which the Scotist school is commonly attacked. First: there is a distinction intermediate between a distinction of reason fabricated by the mind and a real distinction, since distinction by definitions not fabricated by the mind is neither.
claims: There is a distinction intermediate between the real distinction and the distinction of reason.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e963.summary: Second conclusion: there is a distinction ex natura rei that is not real, since what belongs to things by their non-fabricated definitional notions belongs to them from the nature of the thing.
claims: There is a distinction ex natura rei which is not a real distinction.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e975.summary: Third conclusion: several formalities can exist in one wholly undivided thing, since a formality, as its proponents describe it, is the definitional notion of something, and several such notions are posited here.
claims: Plural formalities can exist in one wholly undivided thing.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e986.summary: Reports a variant view: one should not posit plural formalities or concede a distinction, but say only that they are 'non-identical', referring the non-identity not to the extremes but to the composition of the extremes.
claims: Reported view: one should speak of non-identity of composition rather than distinction of formalities.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e995.summary: Meyronnes objects that he cannot understand a distinction or non-identity without extremes of that distinction; it seems to imply a contradiction.
claims: A non-identity without distinct extremes is contradictory.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1004.summary: Explains the variant: its proponent seems to mean that distinction must be referred to the extremes only with a qualification (they are not quidditatively the same in the first mode of per se predication). Meyronnes distinguishes two senses of distinction: as a real relation between distincts, requiring real distinction of the extremes, which is not to be admitted between essence and relation in God since they are really identical.
claims: Distinction taken as a real relation requires really distinct extremes and does not obtain between divine essence and relation.
concepts: first mode of per se predication

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1022.summary: Second sense: distinction as an attribute (passio) of being does not require really distinct extremes but only distinction in some way, and in this sense it obtains in God.
claims: Distinction as a passio entis requires only some mode of distinction and is found in God.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1029.summary: Fourth conclusion: supreme simplicity is compatible with this quidditative distinction, since what is found in the supremely simple is compatible with supreme simplicity, and such a distinction is found in a divine person, which is as simple as the essence.
claims: Quidditative (formal) distinction is compatible with supreme divine simplicity.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1046.summary: Concludes that, from what has been said, the opinions that seemed to be in contention can be reconciled — the dispute was not one of minds.
claims: The apparently contending views on distinction in God can be reconciled.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1055.summary: Turns to two further sayings he does not understand. The first: a divine relative property is so wholly toward its term that it can in no way be compared as distinct to its foundation, a claim meant to avoid a formal distinction between property and essence.
claims: Reported view: a divine relative property is wholly ad terminum and cannot be compared as distinct to the essence.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1066.summary: First of four arguments against it: the essence is as much ad se as the relation is ad aliud, yet the essence can be compared to others by identity and diversity; so the relation can be compared to something other than its term.
claims: Being wholly ad aliud does not prevent a relation from being compared to things other than its term.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1077.summary: Second argument: if paternity, being wholly toward filiation, could not be compared to anything else by identity or diversity, it could not be compared to active and passive spiration, which is false.
claims: Paternity can be compared by identity or distinction to spiration.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1090.summary: Third argument: by the same reasoning divine and created paternity would be wholly indistinct, which is false.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1095.summary: Fourth argument: by the same means there would be no distinction among species of relation except opposed ones, none among disparate relations. Meyronnes concludes that although the quiddity of a relation is wholly toward its term, through another common attribute founded in it — identity or diversity, found in everything under being — it can be compared to other things.
claims: Through the transcendental attributes of identity and diversity, a relation can be compared to things other than its term.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1114.summary: Confirms this by the first complex principle: the relation's quiddity, taken as toward its term, is a being, so of it either 'is the same as the essence' or 'is not the same' is true; on the opponents' view it is not the same, so it is non-identical, hence diverse, since identity and diversity are immediate contraries.
claims: Applying the first principle to the relation as ad terminum yields its diversity from the essence.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1136.summary: States the second saying: the relation as compared to the essence is wholly the same as it, and as compared to its term is distinct from it.
claims: Reported view: the relation is identical to the essence under one comparison and distinct under another.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1143.summary: First of four arguments against it: what belongs to something by its quiddity belongs to it under any comparison, as a definition cannot be lost; the relation by its quiddity, being ad aliud, is not the same as the essence, so under any comparison it remains distinct.
claims: Distinction grounded in quiddity persists under every comparison.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1159.summary: Second argument: contradictory predicates (to be distinguished and not to be distinguished) cannot apply to what is wholly the same; they apply to the relation compared to the essence and the relation compared to its term, so these are not wholly the same.
claims: What bears contradictory predicates is not wholly identical.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1168.summary: Third argument: if the relation compared to the essence is wholly the essence, one contradictory is founded on the essence and the other on the relation compared to its term, so we have contradictories in the quiddities of essence and relation, necessarily according to different aspects.
claims: The view relocates the contradiction to the quiddities of essence and relation.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1181.summary: Fourth argument: the different 'comparison' either adds nothing to the relation (so the contradictories inhere by the same notion), or adds a respect of reason (which cannot save contradictories), or a real respect (giving three respects in one person), or something absolute (as bad or worse).
claims: No account of what the 'comparison' adds can save the view.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1195.summary: Recasts the argument in syllogistic form so opponents must deny a premise: every relative property compared to the essence is communicable; no relative property compared to its term is communicable; so no relative property compared to its term is a relative property compared to the essence.
claims: The relation compared to its term is not the same as the relation compared to the essence.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1211.summary: Second syllogism: no relative property compared to the essence distinguishes the persons; every relative property compared to its term does; so the two are not the same. Then introduces another group who try to save the matter by 'indivisions', with four true sayings, the first being that some indivisions are absolute (by which each thing is undivided in itself) and others respective (by which a thing is the same as that from which it is not really distinguished).
claims: Relative property compared to its term is person-distinguishing, unlike compared to the essence.
Indivisions are either absolute or respective.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1242.summary: Second saying: these indivisions posit nothing positive but are mere privations, as are unities, which seem to be indivisions.
claims: Indivisions and unities are privations, not positive entities.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1249.summary: Third saying: in each divine person there are two absolute indivisions, one of the essence and one of the relation, since each is undivided in itself.
claims: Each divine person contains two absolute indivisions: of essence and of relation.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1258.summary: Fourth saying: in each divine person there is also a relative indivision by which essence is undivided from relation and vice versa, since they are really the same. That there are two first indivisions is proved by the first complex principle: the indivision by which the essence is undivided is in all three persons, but the indivision of the relation is not.
claims: There is also a relative indivision between essence and relation in each person.
The indivision of essence and that of relation differ, as one is in all three persons and the other is not.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1271.summary: Proves there is a third indivision besides those two: the two are ad se while the third is ad aliud, so they are necessarily distinguished.
claims: The relative indivision is distinct from the absolute ones since it is ad aliud.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1277.summary: Endorses these sayings as necessary and demonstrable, but argues against those who reduce the indivisions to a prior non-identity and non-plurality on the side of the substrate. First argument: when a property is adequate to a subject, multiplying the property multiplies the subject; unity is an adequate property of being, so many unities require many beings.
claims: Multiple unities require multiple beings (substrates), since unity is a property adequate to being.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1297.summary: Confirmation: the same privative notion is not multiplied in the same subject.
claims: A privation is not multiplied in one and the same subject.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1302.summary: Second argument: a privation formally inhering in a foundation is found wherever that foundation is; but the divine nature is in the Son without the privation that is the indivision of paternity; so the substrate of that indivision is not the divine essence in the Father but something else.
claims: The indivision of paternity has a substrate other than the divine nature.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1318.summary: Third argument: no privation is repugnant to its foundation; incommunicable indivision is repugnant to the divine nature; so the indivision of relation is not founded in the divinity, nor that of essence in the relation, and so they have different substrates.
claims: Incommunicable indivision cannot be founded in the communicable divine nature.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1329.summary: Fourth argument: things including incompossible extremes (communicable and incommunicable) cannot exist in exactly the same substrate; the indivisions of paternity and of essence include such extremes.
claims: Indivisions including contradictory extremes require distinct substrates.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1342.summary: Confirms all this: it seems contradictory to posit a relative indivision with something while denying it to be toward another, yet every privative relation is toward another, as Augustine says in De Trinitate V.
claims: Every relative privation is toward another.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1350.summary: Gives two syllogisms: no personal property is undivided by communicable indivision, every nature is, so no nature is a personal property; and conversely. Concludes the theory of indivisions is good and true but insufficient unless reduced to a distinction in the substrate. Given some distinction between essence and property, God by absolute power could make someone enjoy the essence without the person, even seeing it clearly. A 'gracious colleague' denied this; his views reduce to four doubtful sayings.
claims: Indivision theory must be grounded in a distinction in the substrate.
By absolute power God could make someone enjoy the divine essence without enjoying a person, even in clear vision.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1385.summary: First saying of the colleague: the essence is not seen without the person because in such vision the essence is the quo and the person the quod. Recast: whenever a nature is the quo of a real operation, the supposit in which it is must be the quod; if this major is false the argument fails.
claims: Reported view: the essence is the principle quo and the person the quod of beatific vision, so one cannot be seen without the other.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1398.summary: First of four arguments against the major in immanent acts: the philosophers' consideration had as formal term the divine infinity and eternity, which are in the three persons, yet they did not know the persons.
claims: Philosophers knew divine attributes without knowing the persons.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1409.summary: Second argument: pagans loved God by natural love, understanding the first nature, without loving the three persons in which that nature is.
claims: Natural love can terminate at the divine nature without the persons.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1422.summary: Third argument: in the Old Testament all believed explicitly in one God yet not all explicitly knew the Trinity by faith.
claims: Explicit faith in one God did not require explicit faith in the Trinity.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1429.summary: Fourth argument: many such persons, in grace and not in error, loved one God from charity, and their love did not terminate at the Trinity, nor did their understanding.
claims: Charity can terminate at God without terminating at the Trinity.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1439.summary: Confirmation: demons intuitively knew the humanity of Christ but not the supposit in which it subsisted.
claims: A nature can be intuitively known without its supposit.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1444.summary: Concludes that the colleague's principle holds for transient actions but not for immanent ones.
claims: The quo/quod principle holds for transient but not immanent actions.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1453.summary: Forms the argument for his own position: when an operation can terminate at a nature without terminating at the supposit, God can produce the first termination without the second; such is immanent action. It is no reply to restrict the rule to perfect operations like intuitive cognition, since the rule applies equally to imperfect and perfect cases, or else it is insufficient.
claims: God can cause an immanent act to terminate at the divine nature without terminating at a person.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1473.summary: Second saying of the colleague: since the nature's relation to the supposit is prior to its relation to operation, and the divine nature is supposited by active generation in the Father, the act of generating precedes the act of understanding in God, so the essence is in a supposit before it beatifies.
claims: Reported view: generation precedes understanding in God.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1486.summary: First argument against: Dionysius says what belongs to the united theology (essentials) precedes what belongs to the discrete (notionals); understanding is essential and generating personal, so understanding precedes.
claims: Essential acts precede notional acts in God.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1497.summary: Second argument: when one thing cannot exist without another but not conversely, the former is posterior; divine paternity cannot exist without the act of understanding, but understanding exists without paternity (in the Son and Holy Spirit); so understanding is prior.
claims: The act of understanding is prior to paternity because it exists without it.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1509.summary: Third saying: against those who hold that the Father, in the first instant (signum) of origin, understood his essence in which he is perfectly blessed before it is communicated to the Son, the colleague says that in God there is no priority 'in which' but only 'from which' (principiative).
claims: Reported view: in God there are no signa 'in quo', only priority 'a quo'.
concepts: priority in quo vs. a quo

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1520.summary: First argument against: wherever origin is formally, there is a sign (instant) of origin; the Son formally has passive generation; so there is a signum of origin in him, a signum 'in quo'.
claims: Signa originis are signa in quo.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1533.summary: Second argument: every distinction is formally in its distinctive principle, as a property in its subject; the distinctive principles of the persons are the signs of origin, so the distinction of persons is founded in them and they are signs in which something is.
claims: The distinction of persons is founded in the signa originis.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1544.summary: Third argument: whatever inheres in a foundation inheres in the supposit in which the foundation is; the order of origin inheres in the signs of origin; so order belongs to the divine persons in those signs.
claims: The order of origin belongs to the persons in the signa originis.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1555.summary: Fourth argument: every relation inheres in some foundation and every relation has some property in it.
claims: Every relation is in a foundation and has properties in it.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1562.summary: Infers that every relation is in another and has something in it, and so is both 'in which' and that in which something is; although a signum of origin is quidditatively 'this from this', it can consequently be in something and have something in it.
claims: A signum originis, though quidditatively relational, can be a signum in quo.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1574.summary: First confirmation: although the whole quiddity of a quality is ad se, it is consequently compared to another.
claims: Absolute quiddities can be compared to others consequently.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1579.summary: Second confirmation: though the essence of relation in creatures is ad aliud, it is also in another. Applies the first principle: either the Father is perfectly blessed in the first signum of origin or not; if not, he would not be blessed of himself, since the first signum is being from oneself. Hence the doctor's (Scotus') argument holds: in the first signum, where the Father precedes the Son, he is blessed and the essence is not yet communicated.
claims: The Father is perfectly blessed in the first signum of origin, before the essence is communicated to the Son.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1599.summary: Further argument: just as the Father has being in the first signum of origin, so he has being blessed there.
claims: The Father's beatitude is co-original with his being in the first signum.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1610.summary: Fourth saying: the property as prescinded from the essence is to be adored, so it belongs to the object of beatitude.
claims: Reported view: the personal property as prescinded from essence is adorable and part of the beatific object.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1617.summary: Argues against it: the notion of adorability is not multiplied, while that of property is.
claims: Adorability is one, whereas properties are many.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1624.summary: Further: in conceding prescission, the colleague concedes a distinction.
claims: Prescission implies distinction.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1628.summary: Further: Abraham saw three and adored one, indicating that adoration terminates in the one God rather than in the plural properties.
claims: Adoration terminates in the one divine essence.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1633.summary: Further: the view seems to posit a personal goodness; but the personal property as prescinded from the essence is not God, and nothing but God is to be adored, so the property as such is not adorable.
claims: The personal property prescinded from essence is not God and therefore not adorable.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1642.summary: Summarizes why the colleague's four arguments fail: the first because its premise does not hold of immanent action; the second because beatitude in the Father precedes paternity (though not as in the Father); the third because the Father is blessed prior and in that prior is not understood to have a Son; the fourth because relation is not part of the formal notion of the beatific object.
claims: Relation is not part of the formal notion of the beatific object.

FrMS88-d1e411-d1e1658.summary: States that the reply to the opening argument is evident from what has been said.

FrMS88-d1e411.summary: The first question of the prologue asks whether a first complex principle can be formed in theology, prompted by Dionysius' claim that all things are both affirmed and denied of God. Meyronnes first explains the principle in itself: through four preambles he shows that it is formed of the first subject, enters the first demonstration, yields the first conclusion, and belongs to the first science; it is most universal, intrinsic to all, most true and most known; there is exactly one such principle. He identifies it as 'of anything the affirmation or negation is true, and of nothing both together', analyzes it as one copulative hypothetical with an affirmative disjunctive part prior to a negative copulative part, with being as subject and affirmation/negation (suppositing for being and non-being) as predicate, and defends this against objections concerning the simply simple, the primarily diverse, privations and fictions. Applying the principle to theology, he argues that it holds formally, univocally, and identically in God and creatures, and rejects the view that divine infinity suspends non-contradiction. This leads to the question's long second half: the principle requires some distinction ex natura rei between divine essence and relation. Meyronnes welcomes a colleague's account of distinct definitions as implying the Scotist formal distinction (intermediate between real and rational, compatible with supreme simplicity), rejects attempts to avoid it by treating relations as wholly ad terminum or as identical/distinct only 'by comparison', and accepts the theory of indivisions only if grounded in a distinction of substrate. He concludes that by absolute power one could enjoy the divine essence without a person, refuting a colleague's four counter-arguments by distinguishing immanent from transient action, by asserting the priority of essential over notional acts, by defending signa originis 'in quo' (so that the Father is blessed before communicating the essence), and by denying that the personal property is adorable as prescinded from the essence.
claims: There is one first complex principle — the principle of excluded middle and non-contradiction in its combined form — whose subject is being.
The first principle holds formally, univocally, and identically in God and creatures; divine infinity does not suspend it.
Saving non-contradiction in God requires a distinction ex natura rei (formal distinction) between essence and relation, which is compatible with divine simplicity.
Relation can be compared by identity and diversity to things other than its term through the transcendental attributes.
By absolute power God could cause the divine essence to be enjoyed without the persons, since immanent acts can terminate at a nature without its supposit.
Essential acts precede notional acts in God, and the Father is blessed in the first signum of origin.
